generators.factoid: The Committee on Public Information's Four-Minute Men (1917–1919) delivered roughly 750,000 speeches in 5,200 American towns — each speech timed to the four minutes needed to change a movie reel. Speakers received daily-updated talking-point bulletins by mail.

generators.factoid: James Montgomery Flagg's 'I Want YOU for U.S. Army' poster (1917) was printed 4 million times — adapting Alfred Leete's 1914 Lord Kitchener original. The U.S. Government Printing Office produced an estimated 1 billion war-bond and recruitment posters across both world wars.

generators.factoid: The Bryce Report (May 1915), commissioned by Britain to document German atrocities in Belgium, contained substantial fabrications — including a long-debunked claim that German soldiers 'rendered' Belgian corpses for fat. Brigadier-General John Charteris later acknowledged inventing the corpse-factory claim in a 1925 New York speech.

generators.factoid: Leni Riefenstahl's 'Triumph des Willens' (1935) shot the 1934 Nuremberg Rally using 30+ cameras, choreographed crowd shots, and aerial photography unprecedented in cinema. The film's editing innovations (cross-cutting, low-angle hero shots) became standard cinematic grammar — Frank Capra studied it before making his Why We Fight series.

generators.factoid: Goebbels' Volksempfänger ('people's receiver') was a state-subsidised radio set introduced August 1933 at the deliberately accessible price of 76 Reichsmarks. By 1939 it was in ~70% of German households; the tuning range was deliberately limited to favour domestic Nazi broadcasts.

generators.factoid: Sefton Delmer's 'Gustav Siegfried Eins' broadcast (1941–1945) posed as a disgruntled-Nazi underground station, transmitted from a manor house in Bedfordshire. Roughly 40% of the Wehrmacht reportedly listened. Delmer's 'Aspidistra' transmitter at 600 kW could imitate Hamburg's signal from a barn in Sussex.

prestige_bridge_copy: 1945 — Berlin in ashes. The dial does not stop spinning. The transmitters built for war find peacetime customers; the script writers find new clients; the airwaves clear, ready for hosts who never break character and never apologize.
